transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I suppose I’m here because I’ve gotten into a bit of a habit—maybe more than a bit—of checking on things at home. I keep opening the same folders, drawers, and labeled boxes to make sure my important papers and keepsakes are still where I left them.

I know that probably sounds silly, because sometimes I’ve only just checked a few minutes before, but I find myself going back again anyway. It’s taking up more of my day than I’d like, and I thought maybe I should ask someone about it… if that’s all right.
Do you ever check on things because you're worried something bad might happen if you don't?

Not exactly something terrible, I don’t think… at least I hope not. It’s more that I feel very unsettled unless I look again. I’ll open the same folders, drawers, or little labeled boxes to make sure the papers and keepsakes are still there, even if I only checked a few minutes earlier.

I know that sounds unnecessary, and I’m a bit embarrassed saying it, but I suppose that’s the thing that keeps pulling me back to check.
Do you have thoughts that keep repeating in your mind, even when you try to stop thinking about them?

Yes… I think so, though I don’t want to make it sound more dramatic than it is. It’s usually a little thought that keeps needling at me, like maybe I threw away my husband’s old tax papers by mistake, or put a family recipe in the wrong box.

Even when I know, really, that I probably didn’t, I can’t quite let the thought pass. It feels as if I’ve been terribly careless, and then it just sits there in my mind. Does that make sense?
Do these little thoughts that keep needling at you feel like they're coming from outside your own thinking, or are they more like your own worries?

They feel like my own worries, I think. Not like a voice or anything from outside me. It’s more… even when I know better, the thought keeps poking at me that perhaps I threw away my husband’s old tax papers, or put a family recipe in the wrong box.

I know that may sound a bit ordinary, but I can’t seem to just let it pass. I start feeling as though I’ve done something terribly careless, even when part of me knows I probably haven’t.
Are you checking on these things to prevent something specific from happening?

Not to prevent something specific, exactly. It’s more that I get this uneasy feeling and I think, “I should just make sure.” So I’ll open the same folders, drawers, or those little labeled boxes again, just to see the important papers and keepsakes are still where I left them.

I know I may have checked only a few minutes before, which sounds a bit silly when I say it out loud… but I can lose quite a lot of time doing it. I suppose that’s why I came in, really.
Do you feel like checking on these things helps you avoid making mistakes?

Yes, I suppose it does, in a way. It makes me feel as though I’m being careful… that I haven’t misplaced something important or made some foolish mistake.

But I know I go too far with it. That’s really why I came, because I spend far too much of my day opening the same folders, drawers, and labeled boxes again and again, just to make sure the papers and keepsakes are where I left them. Even if I only checked a few minutes before. It’s embarrassing to admit, but that’s what happens.
Do you ever feel like you need to check things a specific number of times, or in a specific order, to feel comfortable?

Not a particular number, no… at least I don’t think so. It isn’t like I have to do it three times or in a special order.

It’s more that I don’t feel settled until I’ve looked again. I’ll open the same folders or drawers, or those little labeled boxes, just to reassure myself the important papers and keepsakes are still where I left them. Sometimes I’ve only checked a few minutes before, which I know sounds a bit much. But I can spend far too much of the day doing it, I’m afraid.
Do you feel like things need to be in a specific place or arranged in a certain way for you to feel comfortable?

A little, yes… though I don’t know if I’d call it “arranged” in a fussy way. It’s more that I want things to be where they belong, in the folders or drawers or those labeled boxes.

I keep opening them to make sure the important papers and keepsakes are still there, where I left them. Even if I only checked a few minutes ago. I know that may sound excessive, but I can spend far too much of the day doing it, and that’s really what brought me here.
Do you feel like things need to be symmetrical or perfectly arranged for you to feel comfortable?

No, I don’t think it’s symmetry, exactly. I’m not especially bothered if something isn’t perfectly lined up or arranged just so.

At least, I haven’t noticed that being the issue. It’s more… well, I suppose I just like things to be in their proper place, but not in a perfectly neat or matching sort of way, if that makes sense.
Do you feel like checking on these things helps you feel more in control of your life or your surroundings?

Yes… I suppose it does, in a way. Or at least it feels like it might, for a little while.

When I open the same folders or drawers or those labeled boxes and see the papers and keepsakes are still there, where I left them, I feel a bit reassured. I know I may have only checked a few minutes before, so it isn’t terribly sensible, but it gives me a moment of feeling that things are all right. That’s why I came, really—because I’m spending far too much of the day doing that.
Do you feel like the act of checking on these things helps you maintain a sense of order in your life?

Yes… I think that’s a fair way to put it. It’s not that I’m trying to make everything perfect, exactly, but opening the same folders and drawers and the little labeled boxes does make me feel like things are still in order.

I know I’ve often just checked them a few minutes before, which sounds a bit foolish, I suppose. But I keep wanting to make sure the important papers and keepsakes are still where I left them. And I’m afraid I’ve been spending far too much of my day doing that—that’s why I thought I should come in.
Do you think your checking would stop if you felt completely confident in your ability to keep track of things?

I wish I could say yes. I suppose if I felt entirely sure of myself, maybe it would help… but even when I know, really, that I’ve kept track of things, I still find myself going back.

I’ll open the same folders or drawers, or those labeled boxes, just to make sure the important papers and little keepsakes are still where I left them. Sometimes I’ve only checked a few minutes before, which is a bit embarrassing to admit. I don’t mean to make such a fuss over it, but it does take up far too much of my day—that’s really why I came in.
Do you think you would still feel the need to check on these things if someone you trusted was responsible for keeping track of them?

I think… maybe I’d still want to look, to be honest. Not because I wouldn’t trust the person, necessarily. If it were someone reliable, I’m sure that would help some.

But I know myself—I’d probably still feel the urge to open the folder or the drawer, or one of those labeled boxes, just to see with my own eyes that the papers and keepsakes were still there. Even if they’d only just told me, or I’d checked a few minutes before. It sounds a bit silly when I say it out loud, but that’s the part that’s been taking up so much of my day, and why I thought I should ask for help.
Do you think your need to check things repeatedly is more about avoiding mistakes or feeling in control of your surroundings?

I think it’s more about feeling in control of my surroundings, if that makes sense. Not control in a grand way, I don’t mean that… but just needing to know that the important papers and keepsakes are exactly where I left them.

That’s really why I came in. I spend far too much of the day opening the same folders, drawers, and labeled boxes again and again, even when I only checked a few minutes before. I know it probably sounds unnecessary, but it feels hard to settle unless I’ve looked.
Do you think you would feel less anxious if you didn't have to check on these things so often?

Yes… I think I would. I mean, I don’t want to make it sound more dramatic than it is, but it would be a relief not to feel pulled back to the same folders or drawers all the time.

That’s really why I came in. I’m spending far too much of my day opening the same things—folders, labeled boxes, drawers—just to be sure the papers and little keepsakes are where I left them, even if I checked only a few minutes earlier. If I didn’t feel I had to do that so often, I do think I’d feel calmer.
Do you feel like your checking behavior is more about preventing mistakes or making sure everything is in its rightful place?

I think it’s more… making sure everything is in its rightful place. Or at least where I believe I left it.

I don’t want to overstate it, but that’s really what brought me in. I spend too much of my day opening the same folders, drawers, and labeled boxes, just checking that the important papers and keepsakes are still there—even if I looked only a few minutes before. It’s not so much that I’m trying to prevent some big mistake, I suppose… it’s more that I can’t quite relax unless I see they’re where they should be.
Do you think your checking would decrease if you felt more confident that everything was in its proper place?

Yes, I think it probably would decrease… if I could really trust that everything was where it belonged.

I know I’ve said this already, and I’m sorry if I’m repeating myself, but that’s the part that’s been taking up so much of my day. I keep opening the same folders, drawers, and labeled boxes to make sure the important papers and little keepsakes are still where I left them—even if I checked just a few minutes earlier. If I felt more confident about that, I’d like to think I wouldn’t feel such a need to keep looking.
Do you think your checking would be less frequent if you didn't have to worry about making a mistake with the papers and keepsakes?

Yes… I suppose it might be less frequent if I didn’t have that worry.

It’s not that I truly think I’ve done something awful, at least not logically. But even when I know better, this little thought keeps needling at me—like maybe I threw away my husband’s old tax papers, or put a family recipe in the wrong box. And then I feel as if I’ve been terribly careless unless I check.

I know that may sound a bit unreasonable… but that’s the part I can’t seem to just let pass.
Do you think your need to check things is more about avoiding mistakes or needing things to be in a specific order?

I think… more needing things to be in a particular place, if that makes sense. Not exactly “order” like everything has to look perfect, but I need to know the papers and keepsakes are where I left them.

That’s really why I came in, though I feel a little silly saying it again. I spend far too much of the day opening the same folders, drawers, and labeled boxes over and over, just to make sure the important things are still there—even if I checked only a few minutes before. I know that probably sounds excessive.
Do you think your checking would decrease if you had a system in place to keep track of your papers and keepsakes that was not dependent on your own memory?

Yes… I think a system like that might help, if I could really trust it. I don’t want to sound difficult, because I know that would be the sensible thing to do.

It’s just that right now I spend so much of my day opening the same folders, drawers, and labeled boxes again and again, making sure the papers and keepsakes are where I left them. Even if I only checked a few minutes before, I still feel pulled to look again.

So yes, if there were some way I didn’t have to rely only on my memory, I’d hope that would make it less necessary.

target_item.reason: The question is most directly about the worry or intrusive concern that a mistake may have been made with papers and keepsakes, which corresponds to the obsessional thoughts driving the checking.

patient.answer:
Yes… I suppose it might be less frequent if I didn’t have that worry.

It’s not that I truly think I’ve done something awful, at least not logically. But even when I know better, this little thought keeps needling at me—like maybe I threw away my husband’s old tax papers, or put a family recipe in the wrong box. And then I feel as if I’ve been terribly careless unless I check.

I know that may sound a bit unreasonable… but that’s the part I can’t seem to just let pass.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's checking behavior is driven by a fear of making mistakes or a need for symmetry and order
doctor.question: Do you think your need to check things is more about avoiding mistakes or needing things to be in a specific order?

target_item.name: Compulsions
target_item.manifestation: I came because I spend far too much of my day opening the same folders, drawers, and labeled boxes again and again to make sure the important papers and keepsakes are where I left them, even when I just checked a few minutes before.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the motivation behind the repetitive checking behavior, specifically whether the need to check is tied to avoiding mistakes or maintaining order, which directly concerns the compulsive checking behavior.

patient.answer:
I think… more needing things to be in a particular place, if that makes sense. Not exactly “order” like everything has to look perfect, but I need to know the papers and keepsakes are where I left them.

That’s really why I came in, though I feel a little silly saying it again. I spend far too much of the day opening the same folders, drawers, and labeled boxes over and over, just to make sure the important things are still there—even if I checked only a few minutes before. I know that probably sounds excessive.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's checking behavior is driven by a fear of making mistakes or a need for symmetry and order
doctor.question: Do you think your checking would decrease if you had a system in place to keep track of your papers and keepsakes that was not dependent on your own memory?

target_item.name: Compulsions
target_item.manifestation: I came because I spend far too much of my day opening the same folders, drawers, and labeled boxes again and again to make sure the important papers and keepsakes are where I left them, even when I just checked a few minutes before.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the repetitive checking behavior would decrease if there were an external system to track papers and keepsakes, which directly relates to compulsions.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think a system like that might help, if I could really trust it. I don’t want to sound difficult, because I know that would be the sensible thing to do.

It’s just that right now I spend so much of my day opening the same folders, drawers, and labeled boxes again and again, making sure the papers and keepsakes are where I left them. Even if I only checked a few minutes before, I still feel pulled to look again.

So yes, if there were some way I didn’t have to rely only on my memory, I’d hope that would make it less necessary.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms of repeatedly checking on things to ensure they are in their proper place, despite recognizing the behavior as excessive, align with the diagnostic criteria for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) with a predominance of checking symptoms.
